review_notes.justification: The extension applies validation pools, in which experts stake reputation for or against work, to the trust problem of rented biological compute units.
The extension carries the absence of legal personality for artificial intelligence over to neuron cultures for accountability purposes and names the operating lab as the answering party.
The extension applies the nothing-at-stake argument for staked validation to trust records for biological compute.
The extension applies the repeated-game account of reputation to labs that rent out biological compute units.
The extension applies the non-transferability requirement for reputation to biological compute units.
The extension applies the whitewashing problem of identity-based reputation systems to replacement neuron cultures and adds a provenance link.
The qualification accepts that public regulation remains the framework while holding that participants can build the trust record before rules arrive.

positions.text: Operators of rented neuron cultures record activity, health, lifetime and death. Kaal's position is that this monitoring is the operator's own report and does not establish which units to trust. That requires a record written by validators who stake reputation on their judgments.
scope_conditions: The Register article reports a product launch. It is not an empirical test of these claims.
The position is Kaal's own argument in the essay Who Vouches for a Dish of Neurons?
The position proposes a design for a trust record. No such record for biological compute units has been built or tested.
The position is limited to accountability and trust records for rented biological compute units.
